entities.name: Ummanigash (son of Urtak)
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ummanigash, also known as Humban-nikash II or Khumban-nikash II, emerged as a pivotal, albeit short-lived, ruler in the ancient kingdom of Elam during a period of intense geopolitical upheaval in the mid-7th century BCE. Ascending to power in 653 BCE, he was a son of the former Elamite king Urtak and was installed on the throne of Madaktu by the Neo-Assyrian emperor Ashurbanipal following the decisive defeat and execution of the usurper Teumman. His reign marked a critical phase of Assyrian domination over Elam, transforming the once-proud kingdom into a fragmented client state, with Ummanigash governing one part and his brother, Tammaritu I, ruling another from Hidalu. This arrangement fundamentally altered the balance of power in Mesopotamia, solidifying Assyrian hegemony.

Ummanigash’s installation was a direct consequence of the brutal Assyrian campaign against Elam, culminating in the Battle of Ulai in 653 BCE, where Teumman was vanquished. Ashurbanipal, keen to prevent a unified Elamite threat, strategically divided the kingdom, appointing Ummanigash and Tammaritu I as puppet rulers. Initially, Ummanigash maintained a fragile peace, largely dictated by Assyrian interests. However, the relentless pressure of Assyrian demands and the inherent instability of a divided Elam soon led to renewed conflict. In 652 BCE, Ummanigash, perhaps chafing under Assyrian oversight or pressured by anti-Assyrian factions, allied with Shamash-shum-ukin, Ashurbanipal's rebellious brother and king of Babylon, in a desperate attempt to throw off the Assyrian yoke.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ummanigash's brief reign and subsequent rebellion directly contributed to the final collapse of Elamite independence, leading to the devastating Assyrian sack of Susa and the kingdom's ultimate destruction. His story exemplifies the fate of smaller powers caught in the imperial struggles of the 7th century BCE.
